title: Implement and maintain a HACCP system in a food processing facility

lessons.title: HACCP principles and prerequisites
lessons.html:
What HACCP is

HACCP stands for Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points. It is a preventive, science-based system for controlling food safety hazards. Instead of relying only on testing the final product, HACCP identifies where hazards can occur in the process and puts controls in place at those points. HACCP is recognised internationally through the Codex Alimentarius guidelines, and many South African retailers and export markets require it. In South Africa there are also regulations requiring HACCP for certain food categories; check with your quality department which apply to your facility.

Prerequisite programmes come first

HACCP only works on a foundation of good basic hygiene, called prerequisite programmes (PRPs). Typical PRPs in an abattoir or meat plant include:

  • Personal hygiene and protective clothing
  • Cleaning and sanitation schedules
  • Pest control
  • Water quality monitoring
  • Maintenance and calibration
  • Supplier approval and incoming product control
  • Waste management
  • Training
  • Traceability and recall

If PRPs are weak, the HACCP plan will be overloaded with problems that should have been prevented by basic good practice.

The seven principles

  1. Conduct a hazard analysis.
  2. Determine the critical control points (CCPs).
  3. Establish critical limits for each CCP.
  4. Establish monitoring procedures.
  5. Establish corrective actions.
  6. Establish verification procedures.
  7. Establish documentation and record keeping.

Preliminary steps

Before applying the principles, the Codex approach sets out preliminary steps: assemble a multidisciplinary HACCP team (production, quality, maintenance, hygiene), describe the product, identify its intended use and consumers, construct a process flow diagram, and confirm the flow diagram on the floor. The flow diagram must show every step from receiving livestock or raw materials to dispatch, including rework and waste streams.

lessons.title: Hazard analysis, CCPs and critical limits
lessons.html:
Building the HACCP plan

Hazard analysis

For each process step on the flow diagram, the team lists potential biological, chemical and physical hazards, then evaluates them by likelihood and severity. Only significant hazards need control at a CCP. Others are managed by PRPs.

StepPossible hazardType
EviscerationFaecal or gut content contamination of carcassBiological
ChillingGrowth of pathogens if chilling is too slowBiological
Receiving livestockVeterinary drug residues if withdrawal periods not observedChemical
Deboning and mincingMetal fragments from equipment, bone piecesPhysical

Determining CCPs

A CCP is a step where control can be applied and is essential to prevent, eliminate or reduce a hazard to an acceptable level. A decision tree helps the team ask: is there a control measure here? Is this step designed to eliminate or reduce the hazard? Could contamination exceed acceptable levels? Will a later step remove it? Common CCPs in meat plants include zero-tolerance visible faecal contamination checks before chilling, carcass chilling temperatures, and metal detection on processed products.

Critical limits

A critical limit separates acceptable from unacceptable. It must be measurable, for example a maximum deep-muscle temperature within a specified time, zero visible faecal contamination, or detection of a test piece of specified size. Limits must be based on regulations, scientific literature, customer specifications or validated studies. Do not invent limits; get them from your regulatory requirements, your quality manager or a food safety specialist.

Validation

Before implementation, the plan must be validated, meaning there is evidence that the control measures and limits will actually control the hazard. For example, chilling records and microbiological data can show that the chilling regime achieves the target.

lessons.title: Monitoring, corrective action, verification and records
lessons.html:
Making HACCP work every day

Monitoring

Monitoring is a planned sequence of observations or measurements to check that a CCP is within its limits. The plan states what is monitored, how, how often and by whom. Example: the chiller operator checks and records the deep-muscle temperature of a sample of carcasses at set intervals using a calibrated probe thermometer. Monitors must be trained, understand why the CCP matters and know what to do when a limit is exceeded.

Corrective action

When monitoring shows a deviation, corrective action must be taken immediately and recorded. It has two parts:

  1. Deal with the product: hold affected product, assess it, then rework, re-route or condemn as appropriate.
  2. Fix the cause: for example repair the refrigeration unit, retrain staff, or adjust line speed.

The record should show the deviation, product affected, action taken, who decided, and when the CCP was back under control.

Verification

Verification confirms the HACCP system is working as planned. Activities include reviewing monitoring and corrective action records, calibrating thermometers and metal detectors, microbiological testing of carcass swabs or surfaces, internal audits, and reviewing customer complaints. The plan must be reviewed when anything changes, such as a new product, new equipment, a change in supplier or a new hazard identified.

Documentation

Keep the HACCP plan, hazard analysis, flow diagrams, CCP decisions, validation evidence, monitoring records, corrective actions, verification and training records. Records must be completed at the time, legible, signed and kept for the period required. Falsified or back-filled records undermine the whole system and may expose the business to legal action.

The supervisor's role

Supervisors make HACCP real: they ensure monitors are trained and present, check records during the shift, escalate deviations, and build a culture where workers report problems rather than hide them.

Key points

  • HACCP is a preventive system based on seven principles.
  • Prerequisite programmes must be in place before HACCP can work.
  • A CCP is a step essential to control a significant hazard.
  • Critical limits must be measurable and based on recognised sources.
  • Every deviation needs corrective action on the product and the cause.
  • Verification and honest records prove the system works.
